nodes.label: City governments should close their historic centers to private cars
The change pays for itself in safety, commerce, and civic life
Pre-automobile streets put pedestrians in danger at every corner
Pontevedra removed through traffic and traffic deaths in the zone fell to zero for over a decade
Shopkeepers predict ruin because they assume their customers arrive by car
Retail studies in Madrid and Oslo found foot traffic rose and retail revenue grew faster than in control districts
People linger where they can walk, and lingering people spend money
Closing the center merely pushes congestion outward to the ring roads
A consistent share of car trips simply evaporates when the road space is withdrawn
Zurich measured a third of displaced trips shifting to transit or foot and a share never rematerializing
Residents with limited mobility, delivery services, and emergency vehicles all need motorized access
Permit systems, timed delivery windows, and emergency corridors are standard practice in every successful zone
A historic core is the city's shared living room and does not improve when you park machines in it
Plazas of pedestrianized cities fill with markets, children, and evening crowds
Pedestrianization is not a hardship to be endured but an amenity to be claimed
The cities that moved first top the livability rankings and none has voted to let the cars back in
